text: A mild rheumatoid arthritis flare that matches your usual pattern - increased joint pain and stiffness without new or severe symptoms - can often be self-managed: rest the affected joints, apply heat or cold, and take medications as set out in your care plan. Seek care sooner if symptoms are more severe than your typical flare, do not improve within a few days, or new symptoms appear.

Contact your rheumatology team within 1-2 days if a flare is worse than usual, lasts longer than your typical flare, or is not responding to your usual self-management. Also reach out if you are unsure whether a change in symptoms needs a medication adjustment.

Morning stiffness lasting under 30-60 minutes is common in rheumatoid arthritis and usually manageable at home with gentle movement and your usual medications. Stiffness markedly longer than your baseline, or paired with significant new swelling or fever, warrants contacting your care team.

A newly swollen, warm, or red joint should be discussed with your care team, especially if it is a single joint and out of proportion to your usual flare. A hot, acutely painful single joint with fever can signal joint infection and needs same-day evaluation.

A fever while taking biologics, methotrexate, or steroids should be treated as urgent, because these medications suppress the immune system and can mask or worsen infection. Seek same-day medical evaluation for a fever, and emergency care for a high fever with shaking chills, confusion, or difficulty breathing.

Call 911 or go to the emergency department for chest pain or pressure, difficulty breathing, signs of stroke (face drooping, arm weakness, slurred speech, sudden confusion), sudden severe abdominal pain, blood in stool or vomit, or a sudden severe headache or vision loss. These are emergencies regardless of your arthritis.

Signs of a possible serious infection - fever, chills, a rapidly spreading warm red area of skin, a productive cough with fever, or feeling suddenly very unwell - need prompt evaluation, and urgently so for anyone on immunosuppressive therapy. When in doubt, seek same-day care.

Reach out to your care team about a missed or delayed biologic dose, new side effects, or questions about whether to pause a medication (for example before surgery or during an infection). Do not stop or change immunosuppressive medication without guidance unless you are having an emergency.

Fatigue is a common part of rheumatoid arthritis and, on its own and at your usual level, can be managed with pacing, rest, and sleep. New, severe, or rapidly worsening fatigue - especially with fever, weight loss, or shortness of breath - should be reported to your care team.

Symptoms that worsen rapidly over hours, or a flare far more severe than anything you have had before, should be evaluated the same day rather than self-managed. Rapid change is itself a reason to escalate.

General self-management for a typical flare includes resting affected joints, gentle range-of-motion movement, heat for stiffness or cold for swelling, and taking anti-inflammatory or other medications exactly as your care plan specifies. Keep a symptom note so your team can see the pattern at your next visit.

A useful rule of thumb: if today's symptoms are clearly outside your normal range - new joints involved, much higher pain, or symptoms you have not had before - contact your care team rather than waiting. If they are severe or rapidly worsening, seek urgent care.

New numbness or weakness, new severe eye pain or vision changes, or a new severe headache should be evaluated promptly and are not typical parts of a routine arthritis flare. Treat these as urgent, and as an emergency if sudden and severe.

When it is unclear how serious symptoms are, the safe default is to contact your care team rather than assume it is a normal flare. This tool helps you decide a next step; it is not a diagnosis, and if you think you are having an emergency, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department.
